first_impression.reaction: The 'You Did Not Know?' title is clickbait again. The intro is a bit literary, but the key takeaways give me a dated Smartraveller rating and the registration point, so there's something concrete up top. I went to the FAQ first. The answers are short and some are thin, then I went back up for the detail.

journey.section: Chinese wedding customs differ by family and region
journey.quote: Many detailed accounts come from Singapore's National Heritage Board and National Library Board, and they describe Chinese weddings in Singapore, not every Chinese family.
journey.reaction: Good. They tell me where the detail comes from and what it doesn't cover. Most sites would just say 'in Chinese tradition' and leave it there.

journey.section: Betrothal gifts, hair-combing, door games, tea ceremony
journey.quote: In Singapore, the National Library Board notes that matching horoscopes and hiring professional matchmakers are rarely practised today, while the betrothal gifts are still observed.
journey.reaction: It's honest, but nearly every practical line starts with 'In Singapore'. My partner's family is here in Australia. Is any of this based on Chinese-Australian weddings, or is Singapore just the easiest source to cite?

journey.quote: The four blessings recited are often told, and each family words them its own way.
journey.reaction: 'Often told' turns up in almost every section. I get why it's there, but by the banquet section it starts to look like a way of not answering.

journey.section: What UNESCO says about tea and social practice
journey.quote: The listing does not describe the wedding tea ceremony itself.
journey.reaction: Good. They had a chance to claim a 'UNESCO-recognised tea ceremony' and didn't take it. That makes me trust the rest of the citations more.

journey.quote: When we checked on 6 November 2026, [Smartraveller advice for China](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/asia/china) was "Exercise a high degree of caution" overall, updated 28 September 2026, with higher levels in some areas.
journey.reaction: Dated, linked, and it says the rating straight. That's what I want to see.

journey.quote: Smartraveller also says Australians may be at risk of arbitrary detention, exit bans or harsh enforcement of local laws, including broadly defined National Security Laws.
journey.reaction: A wedding business putting that on a page that's partly selling destination weddings. That's honest about the downside, and it's the main reason I'd trust them on anything else.

journey.quote: For a wedding, look at calmer places well away from those areas, such as the garden and lake cities of the east around Suzhou and Hangzhou.
journey.reaction: Who says they're 'calmer'? Smartraveller's rating is high caution for the whole country, and two lines later they mention arbitrary detention. This reads like their own recommendation dressed up as advice. Either source it or say it's just a suggestion.

journey.quote: Australia is in China's visa waiver program until 31 December 2026, and ordinary passport holders may be able to enter visa-free for up to 30 days for tourism or visiting family, among other purposes; an electronic arrival card is required.
journey.reaction: Useful and dated. But it ends in eight weeks, and anyone planning a 2027 wedding needs to know what happens after that.

journey.section: Paperwork and which office to ask
journey.quote: For the Chinese registration steps themselves, check with the registry and the embassy, including any fees, as at November 2026.
journey.reaction: This is the one practical thing I'd come for, and there's nothing here. They don't say which documents China needs, whether translation is required, or how long it takes. The CNI part is handed back to me as well. It's honest, but it's a gap.

journey.quote: You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law; Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm.
journey.reaction: Clear, sourced, and it admits the limits. Good.

journey.section: Bringing Chinese customs to a wedding at home
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins. The legal steps stay with the registry and the embassy.
journey.reaction: Fee and inclusions in writing, and they say what they won't do. That's the right signal. It still doesn't say whether they take a cut from venues or suppliers.

unanswered_questions: Does Wedded Wonderland take commissions or mark-ups from venues and vendors?
What does the Wedded Advisor fee cover and how is it calculated?
Have they actually planned a Chinese-Australian wedding or a wedding in China? A real example with the budget would help.
What documents does a Chinese marriage registry actually ask Australians for, and does the Beijing embassy or a consulate issue the CNI?
What happens to visa-free entry after 31 December 2026?
Can they arrange a double tea ceremony and travel between two family homes on the day, or is that on us?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Chinese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait headline, and the article is better than it. The orchestrator says the title was set by the person, so this is noted only.

turn_offs_found.quote: Two tea sittings, one for each family, fit into a morning before the ceremony, and a red ensemble for the banquet sits easily beside a white gown.
turn_offs_found.why: Unsupported assertion. Does it fit easily with two homes across Sydney traffic? Says who?

turn_offs_found.quote: When you are ready to shape the day, in China or at home, a conversation with a Wedded Advisor is a calm place to start.
turn_offs_found.why: 'A calm place to start' is a soft sell. Tell me what the first conversation covers and whether it costs anything.

would_share_with: My partner, for the Smartraveller and paperwork section
Her parents, to check which rites their side actually keeps and which dialect group's version applies

cta_reaction.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins.
cta_reaction.why: It comes after the evidence, and 'in writing before any work begins' is what I'd want to see. I'd still look for a fees or commissions page before giving them my details.

top_3_changes: Source or soften 'calmer places ... around Suzhou and Hangzhou'. As written it sits awkwardly against a country-wide high-caution rating.
Add even a short, sourced outline of what Chinese registration involves for Australians, or say plainly that it isn't published and what to ask, and note that the visa waiver ends 31 December 2026.
Cut 'often told' down to one clear signpost per section, back up or soften 'fit into a morning' / 'sits easily', and swap 'a calm place to start' for what the first conversation actually covers.
